summary.text: Alpha decay is a type of radioactive decay in which an atomic nucleus emits an alpha particle, which is a helium nucleus.
The parent nucleus becomes a daughter product whose mass number is reduced by four and whose atomic number is reduced by two.
Alpha particles are very likely to interact with other atoms and lose their energy, so a few centimeters of air can stop their forward motion.

facts.label: Typical speed
facts.value: About 15,000,000 m/s, or 5% of light speed

facts.label: Helium on Earth
facts.value: About 99% of it comes from alpha decay in uranium or thorium minerals

items.prompt: A nucleus with mass number 238 undergoes alpha decay. What is the mass number of the daughter?
items.explain: Alpha decay reduces the mass number by four, as when uranium-238 decays to thorium-234.

items.prompt: Why can just a few centimeters of air stop an alpha particle?

options.label: Its large mass, +2 charge and low speed make it likely to interact and lose energy
Its small mass lets air molecules push it back out with ease
It carries no charge, so it fades out once it leaves the nucleus
Its very high speed makes it burn out in the first few moments

items.explain: Because of their relatively large mass, +2 charge and relatively low velocity, alpha particles are very likely to interact with other atoms and lose their energy.

items.prompt: A heavy nucleus sheds a helium nucleus rather than a single proton. What gives the helium nucleus the edge?

options.label: It is the lightest particle that a nucleus can possibly shed
It carries no charge, so nothing pushes against its departure
It is the only particle that can tunnel out of a nucleus
Its high binding energy means it weighs less than its pieces, raising the energy released

items.explain: The alpha particle's high binding energy means its mass is less than the sum of two free protons and two free neutrons, which increases the disintegration energy.

items.prompt: An alpha particle inside a nucleus has far less energy than the barrier around it, yet it escapes. How?

options.label: The barrier weakens as the nucleus gets hotter
It has a tiny chance of tunneling through at each collision
It gathers extra energy from the neighboring protons
It is blasted out by a sudden violent explosion

items.explain: Decay alpha particles have around 4 to 9 MeV against a barrier of about 25 MeV, but at each collision with the barrier there is a small non-zero probability that the particle tunnels out.

items.prompt: A nucleus with 210 or more nucleons only barely holds together. How does alpha decay help it?

options.label: It adds more protons to strengthen the nuclear force
It makes the electromagnetic repulsion between protons vanish
It stops the nucleus from losing any particles later
It makes the nucleus smaller, which makes it more stable

items.explain: In such large nuclei the strong force just barely counterbalances the repulsion between protons, and alpha decay increases stability by reducing size.

items.prompt: An alpha decay happens inside a molecule. What becomes of the daughter nuclide?

options.label: It breaks away from the chemical environment the parent was in
It stays locked in place by the same chemical bonds
It bonds more tightly because it is now lighter
It stays put because the recoil is far too small

items.explain: The recoil energy, on the scale of keV, is much larger than the strength of chemical bonds, on the scale of eV, so the daughter breaks away from the chemical environment.

paragraphs.heading: What comes out
paragraphs.text: Alpha decay is one kind of radioactive decay. In it, an atomic nucleus throws out an alpha particle, which is the same thing as the nucleus of a helium-4 atom: two protons and two neutrons. What is left behind is called the daughter product. Compared with the parent, its mass number is four lower and its atomic number is two lower. Uranium-238, for example, becomes thorium-234 this way.

paragraphs.heading: Which nuclei do it
paragraphs.text: Apart from beryllium-8, which falls apart into two alpha particles, alpha decay is mostly seen in the heaviest nuclides. In theory it can only happen in nuclei somewhat heavier than nickel, element 28. In practice, the lightest alpha emitter known besides beryllium-8 is an isotope of antimony, ¹⁰⁴Sb. A nucleus with 210 or more nucleons is so big that the strong nuclear force only just holds back the repulsion between its protons. Shedding an alpha particle makes such a nucleus smaller and more stable.

paragraphs.heading: Why a helium nucleus
paragraphs.text: Why does a nucleus throw out this bundle of four, rather than one proton or one neutron? Part of the reason is that the alpha particle is held together very tightly, so its mass is less than that of two free protons plus two free neutrons. That raises the energy the decay gives off. For uranium-232, emitting an alpha particle releases 5.4 MeV, while emitting a single proton would need 6.1 MeV put in. So in some nuclei alpha emission is possible, while other ways of decaying would need energy added.

paragraphs.heading: Trapped behind a wall
paragraphs.text: The real puzzle is how the alpha particle gets out at all. Inside the nucleus it is caught in a trap: the nuclear force pulls it in, and an electromagnetic barrier pushes back at the edge. The walls of that barrier stand about 25 MeV high, but the alpha particles that come out carry only around 4 to 9 MeV. By the old, classical rules, escape is forbidden. Quantum mechanics allows a tiny chance that the particle tunnels through the barrier and appears outside, and George Gamow had worked out this theory by 1928.

paragraphs.heading: A quiet escape
paragraphs.text: In this picture the alpha particle moves about inside the nucleus without stopping, held there by the strong interaction. Each time it strikes the barrier, there is a small chance it leaks out. From this model Gamow derived a link between how much energy the alpha particle carries and the half-life of the decay, a pattern already found by measurement and known as the Geiger–Nuttall law. So rather than being flung out violently, the particle is better pictured as quietly slipping away.

paragraphs.heading: Fast but easily stopped
paragraphs.text: Alpha particles usually leave with about 5 MeV of kinetic energy, moving at around 15,000,000 m/s, which is 5% of light speed. Even so, they are easy to stop. They are fairly heavy, carry a charge of +2 e and move relatively slowly, so they readily interact with other atoms and lose energy. A few centimeters of air is enough to halt them. Alpha decay also supplies helium: about 99% of the helium made on Earth comes from it, in buried minerals holding uranium or thorium, and it is brought up as a by-product when natural gas is produced.
